acids-bases-intro-s1.title: Four solutions at 25 °C
acids-bases-intro-s1.text: A student records one measured quantity for each of four aqueous solutions, all at 25 °C.

acids-bases-intro-s2.title: Ions in four samples of water
acids-bases-intro-s2.html: Key: H₃O⁺ hydronium ion; OH⁻ hydroxide ion. Water molecules and any other ions are not drawn. Boxes 1, 2 and 3 are at the same temperature; Box 4 is pure water at a different temperature.

acids-bases-intro-s3.title: Kw at three temperatures
acids-bases-intro-s3.text: The ion product of water, measured for pure water.

items.q: Find the pH of Solution A from its measured hydronium concentration.

mistakes.why: Value: that is the pOH. pH = −log[H₃O⁺] uses the hydronium concentration you were given directly.
Value: you used ln. pH is defined with the base-10 log: pH = −log[H₃O⁺].

why.correct: pH = −log(3.2 × 10⁻⁴) = 3.495. The concentration has two significant figures, so the pH gets two decimal places: 3.49.

items.q: What is the pH of Solution B?

mistakes.why: Value: that is the pOH, −log[OH⁻]. Subtract it from 14.00 to get the pH.

why.correct: pOH = −log(2.5 × 10⁻³) = 2.602; pH = 14.00 − 2.60 = 11.40. Two significant figures in [OH⁻] give two decimal places.

items.q: What is [H₃O⁺] in Solution C, in mol/L? Give your answer in scientific notation.

mistakes.why: Value: that is [OH⁻], 10^−pOH. For hydronium use [H₃O⁺] = 10^−pH = 10^−9.15.

why.correct: [H₃O⁺] = 10^−pH = 10^−9.15 = 7.08 × 10⁻¹⁰ M, which is 7.1 × 10⁻¹⁰ M: a pH with two decimal places gives two significant figures.

items.q: Which solution has the highest concentration of H₃O⁺?
options: Solution D, with a pOH of 11.62
Solution A, with [H₃O⁺] = 3.2 × 10⁻⁴ M
Solution B, with [OH⁻] = 2.5 × 10⁻³ M
Solution C, with a pH of 9.15

why.correct: Convert each to pH: A 3.49, B 11.40, C 9.15, D 14.00 − 11.62 = 2.38. The lowest pH, D, has the most H₃O⁺.
options: Right: a large pOH means little OH⁻, so pH = 2.38, the lowest of the four.
Solution A is acidic (pH 3.49), but D's pH of 2.38 is lower, so D has more H₃O⁺. A was the only one stated as [H₃O⁺], which is not the same as having the most.
This reads [OH⁻] as if it were [H₃O⁺]. A large [OH⁻] means a basic solution, pH 11.40, with very little H₃O⁺.
A larger pH number means less H₃O⁺, not more: pH 9.15 is basic.

items.q: About how many times greater is [H₃O⁺] in Solution D than in Solution A?
options: About 13 times
About 1.5 times
About 1.1 times
About 129 times

why.correct: The pH values differ by 3.49 − 2.38 = 1.11, and each pH unit is a factor of 10, so the ratio is 10^1.11 ≈ 13.
options: Right: a pH difference of 1.11 is a factor of 10^1.11 in [H₃O⁺].
Dividing one pH by the other treats pH as a concentration. pH is a logarithm, so differences, not ratios, carry the meaning.
This is the pH difference itself. The difference is an exponent: raise 10 to it.
That would be a pH difference of about 2.1, one unit too many.

items.q: Which box represents a basic solution?
options: Box 3
Box 1
Box 2
Box 4

why.correct: A solution is basic when [OH⁻] > [H₃O⁺]. Only Box 3 has more hydroxide (4) than hydronium (1).
options: Right: 4 OH⁻ to 1 H₃O⁺.
Box 1 has equal numbers of the two ions, so it is neutral.
Box 2 has more H₃O⁺ than OH⁻, so it is acidic.
Box 4 has equal numbers of the two ions, so it is neutral even though it holds more ions than Box 1.

items.q: In Boxes 1, 2 and 3 the product (number of H₃O⁺) × (number of OH⁻) is the same. What does this show?
options: [H₃O⁺][OH⁻] is fixed at a given temperature, so raising one lowers the other
Each solution contains the same total number of ions
Adding acid to water adds OH⁻ ions as well as H₃O⁺ ions
The pH of each of the three solutions is the same

why.correct: Each box has 2 × 2 = 4 × 1 = 1 × 4 = 4. This mirrors Kw = [H₃O⁺][OH⁻], which has one value at a given temperature: more H₃O⁺ means less OH⁻.
options: Right: the product is the model of Kw.
The totals differ: 4, 5 and 5 ions. It is the product that stays the same.
Box 2 has fewer OH⁻ than Box 1. Added H₃O⁺ reacts with OH⁻, which lowers [OH⁻].
The boxes have different [H₃O⁺], so different pH values; only the product is the same.

items.q: Box 1 and Box 4 are both pure water. Which statement about Box 4 is best supported?
options: It is warmer than Box 1, because the ionization of water is endothermic
It is cooler than Box 1, because cold water holds more ions
It is acidic, because it contains more H₃O⁺ than Box 1
It has a higher pH than Box 1, because it contains more OH⁻

why.correct: Box 4 has a larger ion product (3 × 3 = 9 vs 2 × 2 = 4), so Kw is larger there. 2 H₂O ⇌ H₃O⁺ + OH⁻ absorbs heat, so a higher temperature shifts it toward the ions and raises Kw.
options: Right: Kw grows with temperature because ionization is endothermic.
The reverse: raising the temperature favors the endothermic ionization, so warmer water has more ions.
Box 4 has equal H₃O⁺ and OH⁻, so it is neutral. Acidic means [H₃O⁺] > [OH⁻], not "more H₃O⁺ than another sample".
Box 4 also has more H₃O⁺, so its pH is lower than Box 1, not higher.

items.q: Suppose Box 1 is pure water at 25 °C, so [H₃O⁺] = 1.0 × 10⁻⁷ M. Box 2 has the same volume. What is the pH of Box 2?

mistakes.why: Value: Box 2 has 4 hydronium ions, but Box 1 already has 2. The concentration is twice Box 1, not four times.

why.correct: Box 2 has twice as many H₃O⁺ ions as Box 1 in the same volume, so [H₃O⁺] = 2 × 1.0 × 10⁻⁷ = 2.0 × 10⁻⁷ M. pH = −log(2.0 × 10⁻⁷) = 6.699, or 6.70.

items.q: What is the pH of pure water at 50 °C?

mistakes.why: Value: 7.00 is neutral only at 25 °C. At 50 °C, [H₃O⁺] = √Kw, and Kw is larger.
Value: you took −log Kw. In pure water [H₃O⁺] = [OH⁻], so [H₃O⁺] = √Kw: take the square root first.

why.correct: In pure water [H₃O⁺] = [OH⁻] = x, so x² = Kw and x = √(5.5 × 10⁻¹⁴) = 2.35 × 10⁻⁷ M. pH = −log(2.3 × 10⁻⁷) = 6.630, or 6.63.

items.q: A student measures pure water at 50 °C and reads pH 6.63. Which claim is correct?
options: The water is neutral, because [H₃O⁺] still equals [OH⁻]
The water is acidic, because its pH is below 7
The water is acidic, because heating drives off the OH⁻ ions
The pH meter is faulty, because pure water reads 7.00

why.correct: Neutral means [H₃O⁺] = [OH⁻]. Pure water makes the two ions one for one, so it is neutral at every temperature; only at 25 °C does neutral fall at pH 7.00.
options: Right: the definition is about the two concentrations, not the number 7.
pH 7 marks neutral only at 25 °C. At 50 °C Kw is larger, so neutral water has a lower pH.
Each ionization makes one H₃O⁺ and one OH⁻, so heating raises both equally.
A reading of 6.63 matches √Kw at 50 °C; the meter is behaving correctly.

items.q: What does the trend in Kw with temperature show about the reaction 2 H₂O(l) ⇌ H₃O⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq)?
options: It is endothermic: heating favors the forward reaction
It is exothermic: heating favors the forward reaction
It is endothermic: heating favors the reverse reaction
It goes to completion at 50 °C

why.correct: K grows with temperature, so heating shifts the equilibrium toward the ions. By Le Châtelier's principle, heating favors the endothermic direction, so the forward reaction absorbs heat.
options: Right: larger K at higher T means the forward direction absorbs heat.
Heating favors the endothermic direction; if the forward reaction released heat, K would fall as the water warms.
If heating favored the reverse reaction, Kw would fall with temperature; it rises.
Kw is still tiny at 50 °C: only a minute fraction of water molecules are ionized.

items.q: A sample of pure water is cooled from 25 °C to 0 °C. Predict the change in each quantity.

variables.name: [H₃O⁺]
variables.why: Kw falls from 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ to 1.1 × 10⁻¹⁵, so fewer water molecules are ionized.

variables.name: pH
variables.why: Less H₃O⁺ means a higher pH: neutral water at 0 °C has a pH near 7.5.

variables.name: The ratio [H₃O⁺] / [OH⁻]
variables.why: Each ionization makes one of each ion, so in pure water the ratio stays 1 at every temperature.

variables.name: [OH⁻]
variables.why: Hydroxide falls along with hydronium; they are made together.

why.correct: Cooling favors the exothermic reverse reaction, so both ion concentrations fall together and the water stays neutral at a higher pH.

items.q: A solution at 25 °C has [H₃O⁺] = 4.0 × 10⁻³ M. What is [OH⁻]? Include the unit.

mistakes.why: Value: you divided [H₃O⁺] by Kw. Rearrange Kw = [H₃O⁺][OH⁻] to [OH⁻] = Kw / [H₃O⁺].

items.q: Solution P has pH 4.0 and Solution Q has pH 6.0. How does [H₃O⁺] in P compare with Q?
options: 100 times greater in P
2 times greater in P
1.5 times greater in P
100 times smaller in P

why.correct: Two pH units apart is a factor of 10² = 100, and the lower pH has more H₃O⁺.
options: Right: each pH unit is a factor of ten.
This subtracts the pH values and treats the result as a ratio. The difference is an exponent: 10².
This divides 6 by 4. pH values are logarithms, so their ratio has no meaning.
The direction is reversed: a lower pH means more H₃O⁺.

items.q: Put the steps for finding the pH of a 25 °C solution from its [OH⁻] in order.
options: Take −log[OH⁻] to get the pOH
Subtract the pOH from 14.00
Round the pH to as many decimal places as [OH⁻] has significant figures
Check: a basic solution should give a pH above 7

why.correct: pOH first, then pH = 14.00 − pOH, then round once, then sanity-check the side of 7. (Kw / [OH⁻] then −log works too.)

items.q: A solution has [H₃O⁺] = 0.0050 M. How should its pH be reported?

why.correct: 0.0050 has two significant figures, so the pH gets two decimal places: −log(0.0050) = 2.3010 → 2.30. The digits before the decimal point only give the power of ten.
options: Right: two significant figures, two decimal places.
One decimal place throws away a measured digit: 0.0050 has two significant figures.
Three decimal places claim more precision than the two significant figures measured.
Four decimal places treat the trailing zero of 2.3010 as measured, which it is not.

items.q: A solution at 25 °C has pH 8.25. What is its pOH?

mistakes.why: Value: you added the pH to 14.00. pH + pOH = 14.00, so pOH = 14.00 − pH.

items.q: Which statements are true for every aqueous solution at 25 °C? Select all that apply.
options: A solution with pH 9 contains no H₃O⁺ ions
pH + pOH = 14.00
Adding OH⁻ raises [H₃O⁺]
An acidic solution contains no OH⁻ ions

why.correct: Kw holds in every water solution at 25 °C, and taking −log of both sides gives pH + pOH = 14.00. Both ions are present in every solution, in small amounts if not large.
options: Right: Kw applies to any water solution at 25 °C.
At pH 9, [H₃O⁺] = 1 × 10⁻⁹ M: small, but not zero.
Right: −log of Kw = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ gives 14.00.
Added OH⁻ reacts with H₃O⁺, so [H₃O⁺] falls.
An acidic solution still has some OH⁻: [OH⁻] = Kw / [H₃O⁺].
